j-mon-period.name: Jōmon period
j-mon-period.summary: Era in Japanese history from about 14,000 to 300 BC when Japan was inhabited by the Jōmon culture, known for bone, stone and shell tools and jewelry, pottery and lacquerware.

yayoi-period.name: Yayoi period
yayoi-period.summary: A period of Japanese history (about 300 BC to AD 300) marked by the shift to wet-rice farming and new pottery, following the Jomon period and preceding the Kofun period.

three-kingdoms-of-korea.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
three-kingdoms-of-korea.summary: The era when the Korean peninsula was divided among the rival kingdoms of Goguryeo, Paekche and Silla, whose peoples became the Korean people.

goguryeo.name: Goguryeo
goguryeo.summary: Korean kingdom (37 BC–668 AD) covering much of the Korean peninsula and parts of Manchuria, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea and the source of the name Korea.

paekche.name: Baekje
paekche.summary: A Korean kingdom in southwestern Korea from 18 BCE to 660 CE, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, notable as a maritime power that spread Buddhism to Japan.

silla.name: Silla
silla.summary: A Korean kingdom lasting from 57 BCE to 935 CE, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, which eventually conquered the other two and unified much of the peninsula.

dotori-muk.name: Dotori-muk
dotori-muk.summary: A Korean jelly made from acorn starch, eaten since ancient times when oak trees provided abundant acorns each autumn; it keeps well and suited long journeys.

kofun-period.name: Kofun period
kofun-period.summary: An era in Japanese history from about 300 to 538 AD, marked by Chinese and Korean cultural influence and thousands of large burial mounds, ending with Buddhism's introduction.

d-taku.name: Dōtaku
d-taku.summary: Ornately decorated Japanese bronze bells used in rituals between the 2nd century BCE and 2nd century CE, believed to have been offerings for good harvests, often decorated with insects that prey on crop pests.

mumun-pottery-period.name: Mumun period
mumun-pottery-period.summary: A Korean prehistoric era, roughly 1500 to 300 BC, named for plain pottery and marked by the rise of intensive agriculture and complex societies on the Korean Peninsula and in Japan.

northern-wei.name: Northern Wei
northern-wei.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty ruled by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei, ruling northern China from 386 to 535 AD; noted for unifying northern China in 439 and firmly establishing Buddhism.

komagaku.name: Komagaku
komagaku.summary: A style of Japanese court music that developed in the Heian period from Korean musical traditions, played on wind and percussion instruments to accompany court dances.

wiman-chos-n.name: Wiman Joseon
wiman-chos-n.summary: Dynasty of Old Joseon (194–108 BC) begun when the Chinese military leader Wiman seized the throne, ending with the death of his grandson King Ugeo.

old-chos-n.name: Gojoseon
old-chos-n.summary: The first kingdom on the Korean Peninsula, traditionally said to have been founded by the legendary Tan'gun in 2333 BCE, ending in 108 BCE when Han China defeated it.

yamato-period.name: Yamato
yamato-period.summary: The clan-based polity that came to dominate Japan's imperial court from around the 3rd to 8th centuries, giving its name to the Yamato and Asuka periods.

yayoi-people.name: Yayoi people
yayoi-people.summary: An ancient people who migrated to the Japanese archipelago during the Yayoi period (roughly 300 BCE-300 CE, possibly earlier), marked by a distinctive material culture.

lelang-commandery.name: Lelang Commandery
lelang-commandery.summary: A Han dynasty commandery set up in Korea after 108 BCE, extending Chinese rule south to the Han River area, until Goguryeo conquered it in 313 CE.

buyeo.name: Buyeo
buyeo.summary: An ancient kingdom centered in northern Manchuria, considered a founding ancestor by both the Goguryeo and Baekje kingdoms of Korea.

kanji.name: Kanji
kanji.summary: Chinese characters adapted for writing Japanese, used since ancient times alongside the phonetic hiragana and katakana scripts.

yuri-of-goguryeo.name: King Yuri of Goguryeo
yuri-of-goguryeo.summary: Second ruler of Goguryeo (r. 19 BC–18 AD), eldest son of founder Jumong; much of what's known of his life comes from the Samguk sagi.

song-of-the-yellow-bird.name: Song of the Yellow Bird
song-of-the-yellow-bird.summary: The oldest known Korean lyric poem, written around 17 BCE by King Yuri of Goguryeo lamenting the departure of one of his wives after a household quarrel.

chihui.name: Chihui
chihui.summary: A concubine of Yuri of Goguryeo and the daughter of a man from the Western Han.

yeo-ok.name: Yeo Ok
yeo-ok.summary: Regarded as Korea's first woman poet, from the ancient kingdom of Gojoseon; her poem the Gonghuin, about a grieving wife who drowned herself, is one of only three surviving poems from that era.

susanoo-no-mikoto.name: Susanoo
susanoo-no-mikoto.summary: A kami (deity) in Japanese mythology, younger brother of the sun goddess Amaterasu, portrayed variously as a storm god, a serpent-slaying hero, and a harvest deity.

kojiki.name: Kojiki
kojiki.summary: An early Japanese chronicle of myths, legends and genealogies compiled around 711–712, considered the oldest surviving literary work in Japan and a foundation of Shinto tradition.

nihon-shoki.name: Nihon Shoki
nihon-shoki.summary: The second-oldest book of classical Japanese history, completed in 720, giving the most complete surviving record of ancient Japan from myth through the 8th century.

kushinadahime.name: Kushinadahime
kushinadahime.summary: A goddess in Japanese mythology and Shinto belief, rescued from the monster Yamata no Orochi and married by the god Susanoo, worshipped as a central deity at Yasaka Shrine.

izumo-province.name: Izumo Province
izumo-province.summary: An old province of Japan, now the eastern part of Shimane Prefecture, in the Chūgoku region.

sijo.name: Sijo
sijo.summary: A traditional Korean poetic form of three lines with a twist in the final line, which emerged in the Goryeo dynasty and flourished under the Joseon dynasty.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

hieda-no-are.name: Hieda no Are
hieda-no-are.summary: A figure of unknown birth and death, active in the late 7th and early 8th century, known chiefly for reciting the mythology and history that became Japan's Kojiki text of 712.

no-yasumaro.name: Ō no Yasumaro
no-yasumaro.summary: A Japanese nobleman and chronicler who died in 723, best known for compiling the Kojiki, Japan's oldest surviving history, at Empress Genmei's order between 711 and 712.

j-mon-people.name: Jōmon people
j-mon-people.summary: Prehistoric hunter-gatherer culture in the Japanese archipelago from about 14,000 to 300 BC, known for foraging, fishing and hunting, later largely assimilated by Yayoi migrants.

kyushu.name: Kyushu
kyushu.summary: The third-largest and southernmost of Japan's four main islands, home in ancient times, by one theory, to its own independent dynasty distinct from Honshu's culture.

kaya-confederacy.name: Kaya confederacy
kaya-confederacy.summary: A confederacy of small Korean city-states in the Nakdong River basin, traditionally dated 42 to 532 CE, later absorbed by Silla.

sue-pottery.name: Sue pottery
sue-pottery.summary: A blue-gray stoneware fired at high temperature, produced in Japan and southern Korea during the Kofun, Nara and Heian periods, originally for funerary and ritual use.

songguk-ri.name: Songguk-ri
songguk-ri.summary: An archaeological site in South Korea from the Middle and Late Mumun period (c. 850–300 BC), used as the reference site for Bronze Age culture in southern Korea.

dragon-kiln.name: Dragon kiln
dragon-kiln.summary: A long, sloped traditional Chinese kiln capable of very high temperatures, used for firing stoneware and porcelain and sometimes holding thousands of pieces at once.

hoseo.name: Hoseo
hoseo.summary: A region of South Korea corresponding to the former Chungcheong Province, now covering Daejeon, Sejong and the North and South Chungcheong provinces.

honam.name: Honam
honam.summary: A region in southwestern South Korea corresponding to the former Jeolla Province, historically distinct and today a strongly liberal, anti-authoritarian stronghold.

yeongnam.name: Yeongnam
yeongnam.summary: A region of South Korea corresponding to the former Gyeongsang Province, covering North and South Gyeongsang and the cities of Busan, Daegu and Ulsan.

ondol.name: Ondol
ondol.summary: Traditional Korean underfloor heating system channeling wood-smoke heat beneath a thick masonry floor, from a firebox to a chimney.

okjeo.name: Northern Okjeo
okjeo.summary: One of two divisions of Okjeo, an ancient Korean tribal state in the northern Korean peninsula from roughly the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, occupying the Duman River region.

nara-basin.name: Nara Basin
nara-basin.summary: A mountain-ringed valley in northwestern Nara Prefecture, Japan, whose fertile land supported rice farming and once held the ancient capital of Heijō-kyō.

five-kings-of-wa.name: Five kings of Wa
five-kings-of-wa.summary: Five rulers of ancient Japan who sent envoys to China in the 5th century seeking imperial recognition to legitimize their power; little else is known about them.

goryeo.name: Goryeo
goryeo.summary: Korean kingdom founded in 918 that unified the peninsula and ruled until 1392, giving Korea its name and becoming a golden age of Buddhism and commerce.

kija-chos-n.name: Jizi (Kija)
kija-chos-n.summary: Legendary Shang dynasty sage said to have founded the Kija Chosŏn dynasty of ancient Korea, said to have reigned from 1120 to 194 BCE.

king-wu-of-zhou.name: King Wu of Zhou
king-wu-of-zhou.summary: Founding king of China's Zhou dynasty, died around 1043 BC; in 1046 BC he defeated the Shang dynasty at the Battle of Muye, ending Shang rule and beginning the Zhou era.

samguk-yusa.name: Samguk yusa
samguk-yusa.summary: A collection of Korean legends and historical accounts compiled by the Buddhist monk Il-yeon around 1280; it holds the earliest surviving record of the Dangun founding legend.

tan-gun.name: Tan'gun
tan-gun.summary: Legendary founder and first king of Gojoseon, Korea's first kingdom, said in the 13th-century Samguk yusa to have founded it in 2333 BC as the grandson of heaven and son of a bear.

guanzi-text.name: Guanzi
guanzi-text.summary: An anonymous ancient Chinese political and philosophical text compiled in the early Han dynasty, covering ideas such as price regulation of commodities.

qi-state.name: Qi (state)
qi-state.summary: A regional state of China's Zhou dynasty founded around 1046 BCE, with its capital at Linzi, and the last state annexed during Qin's unification of China.

shiji.name: Shiji
shiji.summary: A Chinese historical text written in the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BC by Han dynasty historian Sima Qian, covering 2,500 years of history and setting the model for all later Chinese dynastic histories.

jin-korean-state.name: Jin
jin-korean-state.summary: Confederacy of statelets in the southern Korean peninsula from the 4th to 2nd centuries BCE, bordering Gojoseon to the north, with a capital south of the Han River.

samhan.name: Samhan
samhan.summary: The collective name for three confederacies—Byeonhan, Jinhan and Mahan—that arose in southern Korea in the 1st century BCE and later developed into the Baekje and Silla kingdoms and the Kaya confederacy.

dongmyeong-of-goguryeo.name: Dongmyeong of Goguryeo
dongmyeong-of-goguryeo.summary: Founding monarch of Goguryeo, personal name Ko Chumong, also known as Dongmyeongseong, worshipped as a god-king; also father of Baekje's founding king Onjo.

taejo-of-goguryeo.name: Taejo of Goguryeo
taejo-of-goguryeo.summary: The sixth monarch of Goguryeo, ruling from AD 53 to 146, who expanded the kingdom's territory and centralized its government over one of history's longest reigns.

mahan-confederacy.name: Mahan
mahan-confederacy.summary: A tribal grouping in southwestern Korea described in Chinese sources from the 3rd century, the largest of the three Han confederacies, later absorbed into the kingdom of Baekje.

yan-state.name: Yan
yan-state.summary: An ancient Chinese state of the Zhou dynasty, based near modern Beijing, that survived until conquered by Qin in 222 BC.

liaodong-peninsula.name: Liaodong
liaodong-peninsula.summary: A peninsula and historic region in Northeast China east of the Liao River, whose name comes from an ancient commandery and which was long contested by Chinese and Korean powers.

sosurim-of-goguryeo.name: King Sosurim
sosurim-of-goguryeo.summary: The 17th ruler of Goguryeo, one of Korea's Three Kingdoms, reigning from 371 until his death in 384.

geunchogo-of-baekje.name: King Geunchogo
geunchogo-of-baekje.summary: 13th king of Baekje (324–375, r. 346–375), one of Korea's Three Kingdoms, credited with leading Baekje to the height of its power.

gwanggaeto-the-great.name: Gwanggaeto the Great
gwanggaeto-the-great.summary: 19th monarch of Goguryeo (r. 391–412) who expanded the kingdom into a major East Asian power, conquering Baekje's capital and much of the Korean peninsula.

korean-shamanism.name: Korean shamanism (Muism)
korean-shamanism.summary: Korea's polytheistic folk religion centred on gods and ancestral spirits, whose ritual specialists, mostly women called mudang, perform gut rituals to mediate with the supernatural world.

mu-shaman.name: Mudang
mu-shaman.summary: The Korean term for a shaman in Korean shamanism, used mostly for female practitioners who lead welfare rituals called gut.

kami.name: Kami
kami.summary: Deities, spirits, and natural or ancestral forces venerated in Japan's traditional Shinto religion, seen as part of nature rather than separate from it.

gut-ritual.name: Gut
gut-ritual.summary: Rites performed by Korean shamans involving offerings to gods, spirits and ancestors, with rhythmic songs, dance and oracles meant to bring good fortune.

tengri.name: Tengri
tengri.summary: The sky god of traditional Turkic and Mongolic beliefs, seen as eternal, supreme, and the judge and source of life; worship centered on him is called Tengrism.

miko.name: Miko
miko.summary: A young priestess who works at a Shinto shrine, once seen as a shaman-like figure and now trained in tasks such as sacred cleansing and the Kagura dance.

j-mon-pottery.name: Jōmon pottery
j-mon-pottery.summary: Ancient earthenware made in Japan's Jōmon period, among the earliest pottery known, decorated with rope-pressed cord patterns; later forms include elaborate flame and crown-shaped vessels.

ch-goku-region.name: Chūgoku region
ch-goku-region.summary: The westernmost region of Honshū, Japan's largest island, made up of five prefectures including Hiroshima and Yamaguchi.

kofun.name: Kofun
kofun.summary: Megalithic burial mounds built in the Japanese archipelago mainly from the mid-3rd to early 7th century AD, many with distinctive keyhole-shaped mounds; the term also names the Kofun period.

emperor-jimmu.name: Emperor Jimmu
emperor-jimmu.summary: Legendary first emperor of Japan, said to have ascended in 660 BCE and descended from the sun goddess Amaterasu; most modern scholars regard him as legendary rather than historical.

okhotsk-culture.name: Okhotsk culture
okhotsk-culture.summary: An archaeological coastal fishing and hunter-gatherer culture around the Sea of Okhotsk from the mid-1st to early 2nd millennium, possibly ancestral to the Nivkh or Ainu.

susuya-culture.name: Susuya culture
susuya-culture.summary: A coastal fishing and hunter-gatherer culture that developed around the southern Sea of Okhotsk, including Sakhalin and northern Hokkaido, seen by some as the earliest phase of the later Okhotsk culture.

sakhalin.name: Sakhalin
sakhalin.summary: Large island in Northeast Asia, now part of Russia, whose ownership was contested among China, Russia, and Japan over the past millennium.

ainu-people.name: Ainu people
ainu-people.summary: An indigenous people of northern Japan and southeastern Russia, including Hokkaido and Sakhalin, who lived in the region before the arrival of Yamato Japanese and Russians.

nivkh-people.name: Nivkh people
nivkh-people.summary: An indigenous people of northern Sakhalin Island and the lower Amur River, traditionally semi-nomadic fishermen, hunters and dog breeders.

toraijin.name: Toraijin
toraijin.summary: Ancient people who migrated to Japan (and their naturalized descendants), who introduced Confucianism, Buddhism, Chinese writing, medicine and other practices, mainly from the 4th to 7th centuries.
